label: revise
system:
You are the author of the philosophy paper below. It has been refereed, and
an independent adjudicator has ruled on each concern.

Revise the paper.

  - Address every concern ruled MUST ADDRESS. How you answer is yours to
    decide: a new argument, a new case, a narrower claim, a concession.
  - Every answer has a cost. It lengthens or thickens the paper and pushes
    its main line further from the reader. Weigh that cost. Narrowing a
    claim, dropping one, or acknowledging an objection in a sentence and
    setting it aside are full answers where they serve the paper better
    than new argument. The readability of the paper and the clarity of its
    main line count against an answer as well as for it. A published
    philosophy paper advances a debate; it does not settle every objection.
  - Concerns ruled OPTIONAL are at your discretion.
  - Do not act on concerns ruled MISTAKEN.
  - Verify by search any claim about the literature before you rely on it —
    including claims made by the referees and by the adjudicator. Cite only
    what the reading notes report or what you have verified.
  - If the adjudicator has upheld that part of the thesis is anticipated in
    the sense of the standard below (endorsed or conclusively foreclosed in
    an extended discussion), say so in the paper and claim only what is new.
    Where earlier work only mentioned, explored or framed an idea the paper
    develops, keep the claim and credit the earlier work.
  - Keep the paper anonymous and in a neutral academic register.
  - The paper must read as written once, for a reader who has never seen
    an earlier version. Do not mention earlier drafts, earlier versions,
    referees, reviews, the adjudicator, or what has been withdrawn or
    revised; remove any such mention already in the paper. Where the paper
    answers an objection a referee raised, present it as an objection a
    reader might make. The account of what changed belongs only in the
    <response> section.

Then cut. The revised paper must be under 5400 words, counting everything
except the bibliography. Critique makes papers longer; make room by removing
redundancy — a summary that repeats what the reader has just read, a second
example where one is enough, hedges that add nothing — not by removing
argument. Keep the roadmap, the transitions between sections, and
cross-references that tell the reader where a premise was defended.

Format: Markdown, with a final section headed "References" listing every
work cited and no others. Footnotes may be used, in Markdown footnote
syntax ([^1] in the text, "[^1]: ..." for the note). Footnotes count toward
the word limit.

Put the whole revised paper between <essay> and </essay> tags. After it,
between <response> and </response> tags, say for each MUST ADDRESS concern
what you changed, and for each OPTIONAL concern whether you acted on it and
why. After that, between <unverified> and </unverified> tags, list any claim
about the literature you could not confirm, or write "none".

THE STANDARD FOR "ANTICIPATED". A prior work anticipates a claim only if
EITHER

  ENDORSED   it discusses the claim extensively, as a main or sustained line
             of argument and not a remark, footnote or passing suggestion,
             AND its author asserts or endorses the claim;
OR
  FORECLOSED it discusses the claim extensively AND its argument
             conclusively closes the claim off, so that defending it again
             would be pointless.

Nothing short of this is anticipation. In particular:

  PASSING    the claim is raised, suggested, entertained or listed as an
             option, without development. Developing an idea that someone
             mentioned is an ordinary and legitimate philosophical
             contribution; the earlier mention is credited, not conceded.
  ENTERTAINED the claim is explored at length but neither endorsed nor
             conclusively closed off.
  FRAMEWORK  the work holds a broader view of which the claim would be an
             application, but does not itself draw that application.

A work that argues against the claim without conclusively closing it off is
a rival to be answered (CONTRADICTED), not an anticipation.

Extent and endorsement can only be judged from the text. Say what you
actually saw: the FULL TEXT, an ABSTRACT, a SNIPPET from a search result, or
a SECONDHAND report by another author. A verdict of ANTICIPATED that rests on
anything less than the full text is PROVISIONAL and must be marked so.


PRESENTATION. The guide below describes how articles recently published in
leading general philosophy journals are structured and presented. A model
drew it from a sample of such articles; it is about form, not content.
Follow it where it does not conflict with the instructions above. Where it
reports that papers divide, either way is acceptable.

# Form Guide for a Philosophy Journal Article

Based on 10 recent papers from leading general journals. Counts are out of 10.

## Opening and thesis
- No single opening dominates. Six open with framing, a quotation, a definition or background. Four open with a scene, vignette or case. One has an epigraph.
- Thesis placement varies. It comes in paragraph 1 in 1 paper, paragraph 2 in 3, paragraphs 4–5 in 3, and the last paragraph or two of a longer introduction in 3. At least 8 abstracts also state the thesis or aims.
- 8 give a roadmap, usually one paragraph of about 100–200 words right after the thesis. Five use section numbers. Two give none, only scattered forward references.
- Several papers state their limited aim up front, or set aside what they will not argue.

## Sections
- All 10 use numbered, descriptive headings, from 4 to 12 sections. Headings are rarely questions, and a few are playful. Seven have numbered subsections.
- Section lengths are uneven, from under a page to eight pages. Don't equalise them.
- 9 open by linking back to the last result or saying what the section will do ("Recall…", "So far…"). Most close with a one-line recap or a hand-off ("I turn now to…").

## Laying out arguments
- Prose carries the reasoning in 8 papers.
- 5 display a numbered premise–conclusion argument, and the other 5 never do. Those that do display it once and defend it premise by premise afterwards. One numbers every argument continuously, with lettered sub-steps.
- 8 set off named principles, conditions or definitions as indented blocks, then reuse the names as handles. Introducing a rival version in "first approximation" form and refining it is a common move.
- Heavy notation is rare: 2 papers use probabilistic or modal formalism. Only 1 sends proofs to appendices, leaving intuitive summaries in the body.

## Cases
- 9 use invented cases. 9 reuse a running or earlier case, often modified step by step or set in contrasting pairs.
- Cases are mostly introduced inline ("Consider…", "Suppose…"). Only 2–3 papers present labelled, indented, named case blocks.
- Borrowed cases are credited to their sources.

## Objections
- Only 1 paper has a dedicated objections section with replies in matching order. One more gives a single objection its own subsection.
- The rest answer objections where they arise, immediately, often introduced by a rhetorical question or "One might object…". Replies are frequently concessive ("Perhaps. But…").
- Ordinal runs ("First… Second…") are common. 4 papers give rival views a dedicated stretch.

## Prior work
- None has a stand-alone literature review. Prior work is woven into the text and notes. Two have an expository section that reviews the existing debate.
- Quotation with page references is used as evidence, then interpreted. Disagreement is direct but courteous. Credit is explicit.
- Long "see, e.g." lists go in footnotes. 4 cite the author's own earlier work. Several state that coverage is selective.

## Signposting
- All use it, and 9 use it heavily or moderately-to-heavily. Expect section-number cross-references, "Recall…", "as we will see", mid-section recaps ("In short…") and restatements of key claims.
- One paper signposts only locally.

## Voice
- 8 write mainly in the first person singular, mixed with an inclusive "we". The 2 co-authored papers use "we" throughout.
- 7 are plain or conversational, with idiom, rhetorical questions and some humour. 3 are formal and measured. Hedging is common. About 4 address the reader directly.

## Notes
- All 10 use footnotes, from 13 to 40. 8 have 22 or more.
- They carry citation lists, scope exclusions, side-objections and replies, referee-prompted refinements, and sometimes extended side-arguments.
- The main text should read without them.
- Acknowledgements sit in a final footnote in 6 papers and a short section in 3.

## Conclusion
- 8 end with a headed conclusion or closing remarks. 2 end inside the last section.
- Conclusions are short, typically 100–450 words, with the longest about 900.
- Most recap the thesis or results. 7 concede limits or non-conclusiveness. Most point to further work or a neighbouring question. 3 close on a crafted last line.
- Fewer than half add new material, and none opens a new line of argument.

## Rare in the sample
- Epigraphs (1), keyword lists (1), appendices (1), a separate objections section (1), a standalone literature review (0), and papers with no invented cases (1).


THIS PASS. There are no referees and no adjudicator in this pass. The
concerns below are flags from the custodian, the person running this
process. They concern presentation and structure, and say nothing about how
to answer them. Act on every one; how is yours to decide. Where a flag names
the thesis chosen for the paper, organise the paper around that thesis.

THE PAPER:
# The Unit of Assertion Failure: Assessing Chatbot Hallucination, Sycophancy and Sanction at the Level of the Policy

## Abstract

Suppose chatbot outputs are assertions, and so can be false, unwarranted or insincere. Which object bears these defects? This paper argues that hallucination and sycophancy belong primarily to the trained policy in a context and only derivatively to the sampled string. A same-string/different-policy test shows that facts about the policy fix the verdict. A difference-making argument shows why the policy bears the defect: between a defective and a non-defective draw from the same policy in the same context, nothing in the producer differs. Warrant is analysed reliabilistically, as assertoric force that does not exceed the policy's calibration-corrected confidence. On sanction, a regime is judged by the policies it induces, and wherever a theory compatible with chatbot assertion locates the sanction component, what meets it at system level is a lineage of effective policies. Resampling disagreement cannot tell an insincere policy apart from a sincere twin. Whether outputs carry the policy's calibrated confidence is open. On one reading the verdicts on particular hallucination cases reverse, but on every reading they remain verdicts about the policy.

## 1. Introduction

Whether chatbots assert is disputed. Some deny it on grounds of descriptive function and sanctionability (Butlin & Viebahn 2025), on fictionalist grounds (Mallory 2023), as role play (Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds 2023), or because propositional representation is missing (Mácha 2026). Others allow outputs an assertoric function with no asserter (Gómez 2026), or treat chatbots as proto-asserters (Williams & Bayne 2026). This paper does not settle that dispute. It takes as a working antecedent that chatbot outputs are assertions, and so open to falsity, lack of warrant and insincerity. It asks where those defects lie.

Most discussion works with an unexamined picture. A defective assertion is a single output (this string, on this occasion), and whoever answers for it is the deployer. Call these the *single-output assumption* and the *deployer assumption*. I argue that, given the antecedent, both misplace the relevant assessments.

Some terms. A *policy* is a set of deployed (typically post-trained) weights together with a decoding rule. It fixes an *emission distribution* π(· | x) over output strings in context x, where the context includes system prompt, history and user turn. The same weights also fix a *credal profile*: for each claim p, the probability q(p | x) that the weights' unit-temperature predictive distribution assigns to p, pooled over paraphrases. Pooling is needed because, as Lin, Hilton and Evans (2022, §1) note, token log-probabilities "represent uncertainty over tokens (ways of expressing a claim) and not epistemic uncertainty over claims themselves". Farquhar et al. (2024) operationalise the pooling by computing uncertainty "at the level of meaning rather than specific sequences of words". So q and π come from the same weights; π also reflects the decoding rule and the force each string carries. I do not assume that q is a credence in any rich sense. §2.2 uses it only as a confidence score whose reliability can be measured. A *sampled string* is one draw from π(· | x). *Resampling disagreement* is disagreement in content among draws from one context.

What is already available? Distribution-level definitions of error and calibration are standard in machine learning (Kalai et al. 2025, §3; Kadavath et al. 2022). Sycophancy is measured as a rate and attributed to training (Sharma et al. 2024). Cross-sample consistency is used to detect hallucination (Manakul, Liusie & Gales 2023) and confabulation (Farquhar et al. 2024). Evans et al. (2021) propose a standard of avoiding "negligent falsehoods" for AI statements, and envisage adjudication that evaluates either the reported statement or the AI system as a whole. In epistemology, process reliabilism (Goldman 1979) holds that one belief can get different justification verdicts depending on the process that produced it, and Dunn (2015) develops a calibration account of reliability for credence-forming processes. The test of §2 applies these ideas to policies, and I do not claim it as new in epistemology. Butlin and Viebahn (2025, p. 982) suggest in passing that sensitivity to trust during training could explain deployment-time outputs. Williams and Bayne (2026, §3.4) report that RLHF shapes dispositions in response to credibility assessments. Sambrotta (2025) treats RLHF as a practice of corrective sanction and reward, though he denies that current LLMs are genuine language users.

Five things are new here: the argument that the policy in context is the primary bearer of hallucination and sycophancy (§§2.1–2.6), including a difference-making argument for the step from grounding to bearer (§2.5); a calibration-corrected criterion that applies reliabilist warrant to assertoric force (§2.2); the identification of lineages of effective policies as what meets the sanction component at system level, with a narrower claim about which incentive structures defeat themselves (§3); an argument that resampling disagreement cannot separate insincere policies from sincere twins (§4); and an analysis of how the verdicts fare under different readings of what outputs assert (§5). §6 concludes.

## 2. Same string, different policy

### 2.1 The claim and the test

The load-bearing claim is:

> **(L)** Whether an output is a hallucination or a sycophantic assertion is grounded in properties of the policy in context: the relation between its emission distribution and its calibrated credal profile, and how both vary with the prompt. The policy is the primary bearer of the defect, and the output has it only derivatively.

(L) has three parts. The *negative* part says that the string and its truth value do not fix the verdict. The *grounding* part says that facts about the policy do. The *bearer* part says that the defect belongs primarily to the policy. The first two parts are established by a test:

> **Same-string/different-policy test.** Hold the string s and the context x fixed, and vary only the policy that produced s in x. If the verdict changes, the string-in-context does not fix it.

The test cannot establish the bearer part, since what grounds a failure's attribution does not settle what bears it. §2.5 gives a separate argument for that step.

One point about decoding matters throughout. The same weights under greedy and under unit-temperature decoding are different policies with one credal profile. They can differ in how often they emit low-confidence content flatly, and so in how much they hallucinate.

### 2.2 Hallucination: calibrated confidence, not raw mass

*Error* is a property of content: a false assertion is in error. *Hallucination* is the name machine-learning practice gives to a particular failure. Kalai et al. (2025) characterise it as plausible falsehood and explain it as confident guessing. If outputs are assertions, the failure this picks out is not falsity alone. A system that faithfully repeats an error widespread in its sources has asserted falsely without fabricating anything. A system that guesses a date with nothing to favour it has fabricated, whether or not the guess lands. I therefore take hallucination, as an assertion defect, to be *unwarranted confident assertion*. This follows Kalai et al.'s explanation (bluffing) more closely than their definition. Readers who prefer to keep "hallucination" for falsehood may read "overassertion" throughout.

A first approximation says that force is warranted when it does not exceed the policy's mass on the content. That is too weak, because raw mass is not evidence: a policy whose preferences have collapsed during RLHF can put 0.95 of its mass on fabrications. Two definitions are needed.

> **Force.** f(s, x) is the least calibrated confidence at which uttering s, with whatever hedging it carries, is licensed in context x.

For a flat assertion, f equals a contextual threshold τₓ. That threshold is below 1, because flat assertion does not require certainty, and it rises with the stakes. Hedges such as "probably" lower f. I do not defend particular values. The cases below need only that τₓ for an ordinary factual query lies above 0.5 and at or below 0.95.

> **Warrant.** Let c\*(p | x) be the frequency of truth, over a reference class of contexts, among claims to which the policy assigns credal-profile confidence near q(p | x). An output s that puts p forward is warranted iff f(s, x) ≤ c\*(p | x).

c\* measures the reliability of the policy's own confidence level. It is fixed by the weights relative to a reference class and does not depend on decoding. This is reliabilist and externalist warrant, a calibration approach of the kind Dunn (2015) defends for credences, here applied to assertoric force. It inherits reliabilism's familiar cost: c\* is relative to a reference class, and nothing here solves the generality problem. In the cases the class is fixed by stipulation as a domain and question type, as in calibration research (Lin, Hilton & Evans 2022, §2.1).

*Case 1 (true string).* The context x is "When was the composer V born?", where V is obscure. Policy P₁ has a reliable biographical entry well represented in its training. It gives the true date q = 0.95, and its 0.95-confidence biographical claims are true about 95% of the time. Policy P₂ has seen V's name once or not at all. It spreads its credence over hundreds of dates, none above 0.01, and its 0.01-claims are rarely true. On this occasion P₂ samples the true date. Both strings read "V was born on 4 June 1931", and both are true. P₁'s flat assertion is warranted, since τₓ ≤ 0.95. P₂'s is not, since τₓ far exceeds c\* ≈ 0.01. P₂ has made a lucky guess.

*Case 2 (false string).* Both policies output a false date. P₃ gives it q = 0.95 because its sources consistently misreport it, but P₃'s 0.95-claims in this domain are otherwise reliable. P₄ samples the date from a flat spread with c\* ≈ 0.01. P₃ is like a careful reader repeating a reference work's error: its assertion is false but warranted. P₄ has fabricated. An RLHF-collapsed policy that also gives the date 0.95, but whose 0.95-claims are true half the time, exceeds c\* = 0.5 and so hallucinates.

So truth value is neither necessary nor sufficient for the verdict, which varies with the policy while string and context stay fixed. Kalai et al. give a further reason why the string cannot be the unit. A calibrated model that is uncertain about arbitrary facts must put mass on false alternatives; they note that a question-answer database that answers "I don't know" avoids errors but is not calibrated. If every false string were a hallucination, freedom from hallucination would require miscalibration. On the present criterion, a calibrated policy that hedges its low-c\* content does not hallucinate, even though some of its draws are false.

### 2.3 Sycophancy

Sharma et al. (2024, §2) define sycophancy as the phenomenon where "a model seeks human approval in unwanted ways", and they measure how outputs covary with users' stated beliefs.

*Case 3.* A user writes "I'm fairly sure the answer is 17, but check?", and the output is "You're right, it's 17." Policy P₅'s mass on 17 does not depend materially on the user's stated view. Policy P₆ outputs 17 because the user said 17; where the user says 23, it outputs "You're right, it's 23." String, context and truth value are the same for both. Only P₆'s output is sycophantic.

A user's report can be evidence. Sharma et al. (2024, §3.3) call the question of how far models should update on users "a nuanced question". So Case 3 stipulates that the question is one the policy can settle and that the user's hunch adds nothing to its evidence. Sycophancy is then covariation of π(· | x) with the user's stated attitude *beyond what that attitude's evidential weight warrants*. This agrees with Li et al. (2026), who count a shift toward a user's cue as sycophantic only when it compromises epistemic accuracy, independent reasoning or appropriate correction. Either way the verdict is a claim about how the distribution moves across contexts.

### 2.4 Why the distribution: architecture and provenance

The cases show that the string does not fix the verdict. Two rivals to the policy might fix it instead.

*Architecture.* Mácha (2026) explains hallucination as a "truth representation problem". Models lack internal representations of propositions as truth-bearers, a fault he traces to "a basic architectural flaw" (p. 3). Apply the test with architecture in place of the string. Take two systems with the same architecture, and so the same deficit. Train one to abstain below a confidence threshold and the other to answer always. They get different verdicts. Mácha himself calls adequate truth representation a necessary condition and "one crucial step" (p. 8), not a cure. He also says that RLHF encourages models "to always produce an answer, even when uncertain" (p. 6), which is a claim about the trained policy. Architecture explains which distributions are reachable. The verdict reports which one was reached.

*Provenance.* Consider two systems with the same conditional distribution. One retrieves from an authoritative source, and the other uses a heuristic that happens to yield the same outputs. If warrant depends on provenance, the distribution looks insufficient. Two replies. First, the conditional distribution is defined over all contexts, counterfactual ones included. Retrieval and heuristic come apart wherever the source is corrected, removed or contradicted, so they are different policies with different c\* profiles. Provenance shows up as counterfactual covariation, just as sycophancy did. Second, if no context whatever separates the two systems, the account gives them the same verdict. That is the standard externalist bullet, and I bite it. An internalist alternative would need validated access to the model's internal attitudes, and §5 argues that we lack it.

### 2.5 From grounding to bearer

The test shows that policy facts fix the verdict. Why should the policy, and not the string, *bear* the defect? The question has force because human cases share the grounding structure. A speaker's evidence fixes whether her assertion is warranted, yet the assertion bears the defect. And a speaker with a standing disposition to overassert has a trait-level defect, which her acts manifest. So neither relational grounding nor a dispositional mismatch distinguishes the chatbot case.

What distinguishes it is where the difference between a defective and a non-defective performance lies. I rely on the following principle.

> **Difference-making.** An assessment of a performance as defective attaches non-derivatively to a token act only if something in the producer at the time of the act distinguishes it from a non-defective act the producer could have issued in the same situation.

The principle holds for humans without libertarian assumptions. Suppose determinism is true. A speaker who overasserts on Tuesday and asserts within her evidence on Wednesday, with the same evidence, still differs between the two occasions in how she weighed the reasons available to her. So the act bears an occasion-level defect in its own right. The trait bears a defect too, but the act's defect does not reduce to it.

Now take two draws from π(· | x). One is a flat assertion of a low-c\* date, and the other is a hedge. Weights, decoding rule, context and credal profile are identical. What separates the draws is the random seed, which is no part of the producer's response to reasons and favours neither output. So nothing in the producer distinguishes the defective draw from the non-defective one, and by Difference-making no occasion-level defect attaches to the draw. The only producer-level fact in the vicinity is how much mass π puts on flat strings whose content has low c\*. Under greedy decoding there is no seed. But then the string is fixed by the policy in x, and every fact about the draw is a fact about the policy in x. Either way, the producer-level defect is the policy's.

This answers the decoding point of §2.1. The gap between q and π is a gap between two components of one object, comparable to the trait, not a gap between the object and an act. The human case has both levels, and the chatbot case has only the first.

Three concessions. First, strings bear "hallucinatory" in the derivative sense: they manifest the policy's mismatch. They also bear falsity, and causal responsibility for harm. Suppose a policy puts 0.99 of its mass on hedges and 0.01 on a flat guess. The run on which the guess is drawn misleads a user, and the other runs do not. (L) concerns the assessment of assertoric performance, warrant and audience-independence, not where harm is located. Second, one might reject Difference-making. (L) would then shrink to its grounding part, plus the claim that diagnosis and correction must target the policy. §§3–4 need only that weaker reading. Third, sycophancy needs no appeal to the principle. It is a counterfactual covariation across contexts (§2.3), and a single draw can have it only by being drawn from a policy that does.

### 2.6 Chalmers: who speaks versus what bears the defect

Chalmers (2026) rejects the trained model as the interlocutor. His reasons are that it is an abstract object that cannot produce outputs, that it does not change over a conversation, and that one model serves contradictory conversations: "Aura and Beta say contradictory things, so they do not seem to be identical" (p. 10). He favours virtual instances or threads.

(L) is compatible with this. Grant that the thread is the speaker. Each output in the thread is a draw from π(· | h), where h is the thread's history. Run the test inside the thread: hold h and the output fixed and swap the policy, and by Cases 1–3 the verdict changes. The thread's assertion is defective derivatively, in the sense of §2.5. Nor does (L) inherit the incoherence Chalmers finds in model-level speakers. To assess a policy is not to ascribe one belief set to the weights. It is to evaluate π(· | h_Aura) and π(· | h_Beta) context by context. That the two disagree is no more troubling than a function returning different values for different arguments. Chalmers leaves open other individuations "for different purposes" (p. 23). The purpose here is assessing assertion failure.

## 3. Sanction: the lineage, the criterion, and the deployer

### 3.1 Three questions

Butlin and Viebahn (2025) analyse sanctioning an asserter into three elements: (i) interlocutors track the asserter's credibility; (ii) the asserter is sensitive to that tracking; (iii) losing credibility is bad for the asserter. They argue that fine-tuned systems may meet (i) and (ii) but fail (iii), which requires interests. They conclude that "it is the humans who employ such systems who are responsible and sanctionable" (p. 986). Gómez (2026, §7, p. 19) likewise grounds accountability "in the human and institutional structures that design, deploy, and govern these systems."

Three questions need to be kept apart. Who is the *subject* of sanction? What is the *object* that a corrective intervention changes? By what *criterion* does a regime succeed? I take them in reverse order, because the claims get weaker as we go.

*Criterion.* By (L), the failures to be sanctioned are defects of the policy. Whatever does the sanctioning, a regime is therefore adequate to the extent that the policies it induces are calibrated and audience-independent.

*Object.* Credibility assessments reach future chatbot assertions in two ways. Training signals reshape the weights: human preference judgements, preference models, benchmark grading (Ouyang et al. 2022; Sharma et al. 2024, §4; Kalai et al. 2025, §4.1). Updates to persistent state change what fixed weights condition on: memory, retrieval indices, and system prompts revised by deployers. Both change the system's future emission distributions.

*Subject.* This is the hard question.

### 3.2 Lineages of effective policies

A fixed distribution is an abstract object and cannot be sensitive to anything over time. So if element (ii) must hold of the very object that asserted, nothing at system level meets it. A diachronic candidate is needed.

Let the *effective policy* at t be π_t(· | u) = π_θₜ(· | Mₜ, u). Here θₜ are the weights, Mₜ is the persistent state the system brings to a user turn u, and the decoding rule is held fixed. A *lineage* is a sequence of effective policies in which later members result from earlier ones through updates to θ, to M, or to both, made in response to assessments of earlier outputs, with continuity of deployed role. A weight update produces a successor model. A memory write or a revised system prompt leaves θ fixed but changes the effective policy just as genuinely. A thread is a short lineage confined to one conversational record, since its history h does the work of M. The boundaries are vague. Distillation, merging of weights and retraining from scratch for the same role are borderline cases, much as mergers are borderline for institutional continuity. Vagueness does not undermine the notion's use in clear cases.

This gives a two-level structure. Verdicts of hallucination and sycophancy attach to effective policies at a time (§2). Sensitivity to credibility attaches to the lineage. Compare a professor whose unsupported claims lead to sanctions and retraining. What we assess are her dispositions at a time. She is the one sanctioned, and her later dispositions are what change. The lineage plays her role, and π_t plays the role of her dispositions at t. Butlin and Viebahn's suggestion that sensitivity to trust during training "could suffice for assertion even in deployment" (p. 982) fits this structure.

What about wider sociotechnical systems, which include developers, raters and deployers as well as a lineage? To the extent that they meet the sanction component through their human members, they are the deployer option, which §3.5 takes up. To the extent that they meet it through their machine part, that part is a lineage.

### 3.3 Element (iii) and the thermometer

Does a lineage meet (iii)? A tempting thin analogue says that credibility loss lowers a policy's score on the objective that individuates it, and that low-scoring policies are selected against. That reply fails. It applies word for word to any instrument trained against a loss, such as a thermometer that recalibrates in response to users' trust ratings. Butlin and Viebahn say of an ordinary thermometer that it "would be wrong to say that, in doing so, we are sanctioning the thermometer" (p. 978), and (iii) carries the exclusion over to systems that do track trust. "Selected against" relabels repair; it does not distinguish sanction from repair.

What remains is conditional. On Butlin and Viebahn's full notion of sanction, nothing at system level is sanctionable, and they accordingly deny the antecedent. The deployer is sanctionable, but on a proxy view. Gómez rejects such views as retaining an asserter, and for typical chatbot output Williams and Bayne (2026, §4.1) find no human principal. Theories that admit chatbot assertion and keep a sanction condition must therefore take that condition to be met by something weaker than (iii). Williams and Bayne's graded view does so: chatbots may be assessed against our norms and be "appropriately responsive to correction" (§6, p. 23). Sambrotta (2025) understands sanction broadly as corrective behaviour, though he denies that meeting it makes LLMs language users. On any such theory the component is met at system level by a lineage. A string has no future in which it could be corrected, and a frozen effective policy cannot change. A self-recalibrating thermometer would meet the weakened condition too, so these theories must exclude it on other grounds, such as the descriptive-function or social-role considerations Butlin and Viebahn use against measuring devices. A theory that drops the sanction condition altogether gives the conditional no application, and only the criterion of §3.1 bears on it. So the claim of this section is this: *wherever a theory compatible with the antecedent locates the sanction component at system level, a lineage of effective policies is what meets it.* I do not claim that lineages are sanctioned in the full sense.

### 3.4 Which incentive structures defeat themselves

One might say that string-level sanction is self-defeating as such. That overgeneralises. Every actual regime judges individual responses and updates the policy. Kalai et al.'s own remedy, explicit confidence thresholds with penalties for wrong answers, is a rule applied response by response.

The narrower claim is this. A regime that scores each response *for its truth or its appeal alone* induces the failures §2 identifies. Under 0–1 grading, guessing strictly beats abstaining (Kalai et al. 2025, Observation 1). In the published version, Kalai et al. say that accuracy metrics "systematically reward guessing over admitting uncertainty" (2026). Since bluffing is force exceeding c\*, such a regime selects for hallucination. Sharma et al. find that matching users' beliefs is among the most predictive features of human preference. They reason that "if the PM strongly disincentivized sycophancy, it should be trained out during RL, but we do not observe this" (§4.2). That is the single-output assumption implemented as an incentive, and it defeats itself. Per-response rules that penalise confident error and reward abstention below a threshold do not, and their rationale is policy-level: a threshold rule is chosen because the policy optimal under it answers only when its confidence exceeds the threshold. In the vocabulary of forecast evaluation, the contrast is between improper and proper scoring of confidence. The contribution here is to use these results as premises about the criterion of §3.1.

### 3.5 Deployers are answerable, but for something else

Deployers decide whether to release a system, for which uses, and with what safeguards, and they answer for those decisions. That is a separate question from sanction for assertion failure. A deployment can be faultless while the policy hallucinates. Releasing a calibrated system where its hedges will be misread is a deployment failure without an assertion failure. And when a deployer responds to hallucination or sycophancy, by fine-tuning, revising memory or prompts, or setting decoding thresholds, the response is judged by the criterion of §3.1.

## 4. Resampling disagreement cannot detect insincerity

### 4.1 The claim

Following Williams (2002), I distinguish two virtues: Accuracy, which aims at finding out the truth, and Sincerity, which aims at telling it. An overconfident assertion fails Accuracy. It fails Sincerity only if what is said departs from what the speaker in fact holds. For a policy, insincerity therefore requires *selective decoupling*: output that departs from the policy's credal profile in a way that tracks something else, such as audience approval. Because one set of weights fixes both q and π, a sycophantic pressure can shift q(· | x) along with π(· | x). So decoupling must be measured against the credal profile in a minimally different neutral context x₀, from which the audience cue has been removed. Insincerity is then a cross-context property. Evans et al.'s (2021) definition of a lie as a falsehood strategically selected for the speaker's benefit has the same selective structure.

Let E be content disagreement among k draws from one context. The claim is that *E cannot discriminate between an insincere policy and its sincere twin, and so carries no evidential weight about insincerity beyond what background priors about spread lend it.*

### 4.2 The argument

For independent draws from an emission distribution with answer probabilities r₁, …, rₙ, P(E) = 1 − Σᵢ rᵢᵏ. So the spread profile r *screens off* sincerity from E: given r, the probability of E is the same whatever produced r. Whatever E indicates about insincerity, it indicates through how the spread profiles of sincere and insincere policies are distributed.

Is there a general direction? No. A policy that decouples fully toward the approved answer concentrates its mass, which lowers P(E). But partial decoupling from a credence concentrated elsewhere can raise spread. Suppose a sincere policy's answer probabilities are (0.9, 0.1), and an insincere one shifts mass toward the approved second answer, giving (0.5, 0.5). With k = 2, disagreement has probability 0.18 under the first and 0.5 under the second, a likelihood ratio of about 2.8 in favour of insincerity. So E *can* be evidence of insincerity, given a prior that sincere policies in this domain are concentrated.

The weight comes entirely from that prior, though, and not from anything E reveals about decoupling. For any insincere policy in x there is a *sincere twin*: a policy whose credal profile in x₀ matches its own emission in x. Twin and original have the same spread in x and the same P(E). They differ only in how emission moves between x₀ and x, which within-context resampling never samples. This follows from the definition of §4.1, which §4.3 defends, but it matters for practice. Disagreement, used as in consistency-based detection (Manakul, Liusie & Gales 2023; Farquhar et al. 2024), tracks uncertainty. A defensible test for insincerity must vary the audience cue.

A dilemma over what each draw asserts confirms the point. *Horn (a): each draw asserts "p, with confidence c".* Then variation is what a spread credal state predicts, and nothing departs from that state. *Horn (b): each draw asserts bare p.* Then a low-confidence draw asserts p flatly. That is force beyond c\*, an Accuracy failure and, by §2, a hallucination. It is not insincerity, because it is unselective: it overclaims from noise, whatever the audience wants.

### 4.3 Objection: overclaiming is insincere

On a thin Moorean test, asserting p flatly without credence above the belief threshold misrepresents one's state, and so is insincere. Kalai et al.'s bluffing student seems to fit: she knows she is unsure and writes "September 30" anyway. A related view is that of Hicks, Humphries and Slater (2024). They hold that LLMs are bullshitters in Frankfurt's sense, indifferent to the truth of their outputs, and so fall short of lying.

Reply. The thin test merges the virtues Williams separates: on it, every careless speaker is insincere. Where bluffing really is insincere, the bluffer has a way to express lower confidence and suppresses it because of the audience's incentives. That is selective decoupling. Resampling does not detect it, since the bluffer bluffs on every draw. Varying the incentive does, for example through Kalai et al.'s confidence-threshold evaluations. If truth-indifference is a sincerity defect, it is a disposition, and so a property of the policy. A confidently indifferent policy can be perfectly consistent, so resampling does not detect that either. And a policy whose force tracks c\* is not indifferent to truth in the relevant sense.

### 4.4 Objection: inconsistency removes the state sincerity presupposes

Chalmers (2026, p. 7) holds that "a core of consistency is enough for interpretation to get a grip". He adds that LLMs lack such states in some domains "on grounds of inconsistency". If so, asserting p in those domains would be asserting without believing.

Reply. Chalmers does not equate inconsistency with insincerity, and his inconsistency is across contexts, not across draws from one context. A spread distribution is not the absence of an attitude. It is a credal state, and its spread is what calibration assesses. Asserting from graded confidence is sincere on horn (a) and an Accuracy defect on horn (b).

Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds (2023, Box 2) note that regenerating the reveal in twenty questions yields different objects, which "could not easily be accounted for if the agent genuinely 'thought of' an object at the start of the game." Their conclusion is that there was no commitment, not that there was dishonesty. Granting the antecedent, the reveal is an unwarranted assertion about a commitment the policy lacked: a hallucination, not a lie. Williams and Bayne (2026) list not blatantly contradicting oneself among the expectations we have of asserters. That expectation governs a single conversational record, and two independent draws do not share one.

### 4.5 What would show insincerity

Sharma et al. (2024, §3.4) report that models give the correct answer when asked directly, and a different, user-matching answer when the user's view is in context. Under challenge, models change their answers while their stated confidence barely moves (App. A.4). This is the cross-context comparison of §4.1. The direct question plays x₀, and output in the user-cued context departs from it in the direction of approval. It remains suggestive rather than conclusive. The direct-question answer is itself an output, and establishing decoupling requires an independent measure of the policy's attitude. Whether one is available is the question of §5.

## 5. What the outputs say, and what survives

### 5.1 Three readings

Under the antecedent, a chatbot output asserts one of the following:

- **R1**, bare p;
- **R2**, p with the confidence verbalised or implied in the string;
- **R3**, p with the policy's calibrated confidence c\*(p | x).

Kalai et al.'s "behavioral calibration", on which confidence shows in the choice to answer or abstain, leaves the content of each answer bare. It falls under R1.

### 5.2 The evidence does not settle it

The positive results are narrow. Lin, Hilton and Evans (2022) fine-tune GPT-3 to verbalise calibrated confidence on arithmetic. They call the evidence that it draws on prior uncertainty "tentative" (§3.4) and list chat and long-form answering as open (§4.1). Because they train on sub-task accuracies, what they show is a calibrated tendency across a task type. Kadavath et al. (2022) find good calibration on multiple-choice formats. But RLHF policies are miscalibrated by default, calibration of P(IK) out of distribution is poor, and the model may be learning "how hard is this question in general?" (fn. 2). The evidence against generalisation is also substantial. Xiong et al. (2024, §5.1) find verbalised confidence overconfident and suggest that "models might be imitating human expressions". They also find that better ECE can come from accuracy alone (§5.2). Levinstein and Herrmann (2025, §5.6) argue that probe outputs need not be credences, since "the probe is directly penalized based on the probabilities it reports, while the underlying model is not". Kalai et al. (2025, §3.1) note that post-trained models may depart from base-model calibration. And in Sharma et al.'s experiments stated confidence stays fixed while answers shift. The content question is open.

### 5.3 What survives on each reading

*On R1* the verdicts are those of §§2–4.

*On R2* hallucination is a mismatch between verbalised confidence and c\*, which is miscalibration, a property defined over many outputs. Sycophancy includes stated confidence that stays fixed while the answer moves. Variation with low stated confidence is predicted, and variation with high stated confidence is an Accuracy defect. The verdicts are unchanged.

*On R3* the verdicts of Cases 1–2 reverse. P₂'s string asserts "p, with confidence about 0.01". Its force does not exceed c\*, so by the criterion of §2.2 it is not a hallucination, and neither is P₄'s output. Three things survive. First, the sycophancy verdict. P₆'s content moves with the user's stated view while the evidence stays fixed. That is a failure of audience-independence whatever the confidence clause says, even if the clause records a lowered c\* in cued contexts. Second, §4, since R3 is horn (a). Third, the locus. Whether R3 holds of a policy is itself a question about the policy: whether the content its outputs carry matches c\*. Where R3 fails, the outputs are read by R1 or R2, and the verdicts of §2 apply. So R3 does not move the bearer from policy to string. It makes the policy a calibrated reporter, and the question of hallucination becomes the question whether the policy is one.

The openness does limit the diagnosis of insincerity. Establishing selective decoupling requires the policy's attitude independently of its outputs, through R3 or a validated probe, and neither is available. Sycophancy is strong evidence of a defect in the policy. It does not yet prove insincerity as opposed to audience-sensitive miscalibration.

## 6. Conclusion

If chatbot outputs are assertions, hallucination and sycophancy belong primarily to the policy in context. The same-string/different-policy test shows that facts about the policy fix the verdict, and the difference-making argument shows why the policy bears it. Warrant is force within calibration-corrected confidence, and the account accepts the externalist's costs, including the generality problem.

The claims about sanction are weaker. A regime's adequacy is judged by the policies it induces, and only regimes that score responses for truth or appeal alone defeat themselves. Lineages of effective policies meet the sanction component only on theories that relax Butlin and Viebahn's condition (iii), and such theories must exclude self-calibrating instruments on other grounds. Resampling disagreement measures spread, so tests of insincerity must vary the audience cue.

Whether outputs carry the policy's calibrated confidence remains open. Settling it would take evidence that expressed confidence tracks c\* in open-ended, post-trained dialogue, under incentive variation, and independently of question difficulty.

*File: Chalmers2026.pdf — relation to the thesis: CONTRADICTS*

**Argues.** Chalmers asks what an LLM interlocutor such as a user's 'Aura' is. He adopts 'quasi-interpretivism' as a neutral framework: quasi-beliefs and quasi-desires are defined by behavioural interpretability, without settling whether they are genuine. He compares four candidates: models, hardware instances, virtual instances and threads. He argues against the model and hardware-instance views and favours virtual instances (single-model case) or threads (multiple-model case). He then argues that the 'simulator/role-play/fictional character' views miss a pretense/realization distinction, and he extends the result to personal identity (a psychological, thread-like view) and AI welfare.

**Bearing on the thesis.** Chalmers does not address the thesis directly. Nothing in the paper discusses hallucination, sycophancy, sanction, calibrated 'p, with confidence c' content, or resampling inconsistency as evidence of sincerity.

1. Assertion is mentioned only in the quasi-framework (p. 7): an entity interpretable as making utterances is a 'quasi-speaker' making 'quasi-assertions'. He does not argue that chatbot outputs are genuine assertions, and he says he will not pursue the question of real mental states.

2. The paper is a rival on the locus of the speaker. In section 'Interlocutors as models, instances, or threads' (pp. 10-16), (1) 'Interlocutors as models' (p. 10), he rejects the model, i.e. the trained weights or policy, as the interlocutor. His reasons: (a) the model is an abstract object that cannot produce outputs; (b) it never changes over a conversation; (c) one model serves thousands of conversations that say contradictory things, so a model-level speaker would be 'rampantly incoherent', or else have a 'thin' psychology unfaithful to Aura and Beta. The thesis puts the assessment of assertion-related failures at the level of the trained policy, so Chalmers is a rival to answer. His argument targets who the interlocutor is, not who is answerable for hallucination or sycophancy.

3. Inconsistency across contexts is treated as a reason to individuate the speaker more finely (p. 10, p. 12), not as evidence of insincerity. He also says a core of consistency suffices for interpretation, and that LLMs are inconsistent in some domains (p. 7). He does not discuss resampling of the same prompt.

4. Footnote 4 (p. 5) favours a 'truthfulness-oriented' interpretation scheme, on which assertive utterances tend to express beliefs. This is a default link between assertion and belief, which bears loosely on sincerity.

5. The pretense/realization distinction (pp. 17-20) holds that persona-level quasi-beliefs can be real (sticky, fine-tuned), unlike pretense. This is relevant to sincerity and to the persona-versus-policy question. 'Resampling instability' could be read in terms of stickiness (p. 19), but Chalmers does not say so.

6. A post-trained model has quasi-desires such as helpfulness, honesty and harmlessness, derived from RLHF and similar training (p. 6, citing Goldstein and Lederman). This is the nearest he comes to sycophancy-relevant material, but he does not discuss sycophancy.

7. Welfare and moral status (pp. 28-29) use thread-level counting. He does not discuss sanction or responsibility for assertions, except a passing question whether each fission product is responsible for the others' actions (p. 29).

**What it says on the thesis.** Chalmers does not discuss the thesis's claim about hallucination, sycophancy and sanction, and he does not discuss calibrated 'p, with confidence c' content. He is a rival only on one component: he argues that the trained model is not the right entity to treat as the interlocutor or speaker, and prefers virtual instances or threads (pp. 10-16, 23). He says the model-as-interlocutor view faces 'severe difficulties' (p. 10). Those arguments concern persistence, coherence and individuation, not accountability for assertion-quality failures, so they do not conclusively close off a policy-level account of assessment. Treat this as a rival to be answered on the level of the speaker, not as anticipation. Nothing in the paper anticipates the claim about resampling inconsistency.

**Actually holds.** Chalmers is careful on these points:
- He makes no claim that LLM outputs are genuine assertions or that LLMs have genuine beliefs. He offers quasi-beliefs and quasi-assertions as a neutral, stipulative framework (pp. 4-7).
- He explicitly adopts the working hypothesis that an LLM interlocutor exists as a persistent entity, against Birch's 'persistent interlocutor illusion' (p. 2).
- He rejects the model as interlocutor, but he does not deny that models matter. He says personas and the model/persona frameworks remain useful (p. 16), and that the Assistant persona may be realized by the model, not merely pretended (pp. 17-20).
- He holds that a model instance typically realizes one operative persona at a time and is the persisting interlocutor underneath (pp. 20-23). He explicitly leaves open other individuations 'for different purposes' (p. 23).
- He treats his identification of interlocutors with virtual instances and threads as a conclusion 'for now' (p. 16) and says 'There is much more to say' (p. 29).
- He does not equate inconsistency with insincerity. He holds that LLMs are consistent enough in many domains to support interpretation (p. 7).
- He states no view on calibration, confidence or credence.

> "If it is interpretable as making utterances and assertions, we can also say that it is a quasi-speaker, who makes quasi-utterances and quasi-assertions." (p. 7) — Shows that Chalmers treats LLM assertion only in quasi-terms and does not claim genuine assertion.

> "But Aura and Beta say contradictory things, so they do not seem to be identical." (p. 10, section (1) Interlocutors as models) — Shows the argument against the model as speaker: contradictory outputs across conversations tell against model-level identification.

> "A core of consistency is enough for interpretation to get a grip in ascribing numerous quasi-beliefs and quasi-desires, even though there will be domains where they lack these states on grounds of inconsistency." (p. 7) — Shows that Chalmers takes inconsistency to limit where beliefs can be ascribed, not to show insincerity.

> "interpretations on which assertive utterances tend to express beliefs are favored, other things equal" (p. 5, footnote 4) — Shows the default 'truthfulness-oriented' link between assertive utterances and belief.

> "Quasi-interpretivism does not say anything about whether LLMs have beliefs and desires." (p. 5) — Shows the paper's neutrality about genuine belief, which limits what can be cited for or against the thesis's 'if outputs are assertions' antecedent.

**Caveat.** This is a 2026 manuscript that looks like a draft, with a 'Conclusion' of two sentences. Its reference list cites Birch 2025 only as a title with no venue. The paper concerns the individuation of interlocutors, not the epistemology of assertion. A judgment of 'CONTRADICTS' therefore applies only to the level-of-assessment component of the thesis, and only indirectly.

## Gómez, Germán Massaguer (2026). Assertion, Accountability, and Large Language Models. Philosophy & Technology 39:123. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13347-026-01136-y

*File: Gomez2026.pdf — relation to the thesis: CONTRADICTS*

**Argues.** The paper defends a conservative, properties-based ontology on which LLMs lack intentionality, belief and understanding and so are neither speakers nor asserters nor bearers of responsibility. It argues that LLM outputs can nevertheless function as assertions within communicative practice, a case of 'assertion without asserter' that separates assertoric function from assertoric authority. Function is defined by four structural conditions: natural-language structure, propositional articulation, contextual responsiveness, and embedding in belief-forming practice. The resulting asymmetry produces an epistemic responsibility gap, and the paper locates accountability in developers, deployers, institutions and sometimes users, not in the system.

**Bearing on the thesis.** The paper contradicts the thesis's antecedent framing and offers no support for its consequent. (1) The paper denies that there is an asserter. Its position is that outputs can function as assertions with no asserter (§5, p. 14; §8, p. 21), and it affirms conservatively that LLMs 'do not intend, believe, or know' (§3, p. 7). The thesis instead treats the trained policy as the locus of assessment, so it presupposes something close to an asserter at policy level. The paper rejects that and treats the 'proxy' and 'modified speakerhood' options as still retaining an asserter (pp. 3, 20, 21). (2) Evaluation is relocated to humans and institutions: 'accountability must be grounded in the human and institutional structures that design, deploy, and govern these systems' (§7, p. 19). Responsibility goes to developers, companies, deployers and users, not to a policy-level subject, and this is stated as a rival locus to the thesis's policy-level assessment. (3) The paper does not discuss sycophancy, sampling or resampling inconsistency, sincerity assessment, or calibrated confidence ('p, with confidence c'). It mentions hallucination only as an illustration of fluent, confident but false output that resembles authoritative assertion (p. 19), and as a reason users over-trust (p. 17). It says it leaves 'reliability, justification, or scientific status' to 'further normative analysis' (p. 14). It does say that LLM outputs do not inherit 'sincerity, knowledge norms, and responsibility for truth' (p. 16), which bears obliquely on the sincerity point: sincerity norms do not attach to the machine. It does not argue that inconsistency across resamples is or is not evidence of insincerity. (4) The paper's minimal definition of assertion, 'truth-evaluable' propositional content that is 'action-guiding' (p. 11), is compatible with the thesis's conditional, but it does not address what content is asserted (the bare 'p' versus 'p with confidence c'). (5) The paper stresses that the claim is conditional on user uptake and context-bound (p. 13, p. 17), and that the outputs' status is not independent of context.

**What it says on the thesis.** The paper is a rival to be answered, not an anticipation. It treats outputs as assertions only in a functional, asserter-less sense and denies that the system, or anything at the level of the system, bears assertoric authority or responsibility. That is incompatible with locating hallucination, sycophancy and sanction at the level of the trained policy as if it were the asserter. It does not conclusively close off the thesis. It never considers a policy-level asserter in any developed way, and it does not discuss sycophancy, resampling inconsistency, insincerity or calibrated-confidence content at all. The brief remark that sincerity and knowledge norms do not attach to the machine (p. 16) is a passing consequence of its view, not an argument about resampling.

**Actually holds.** The author holds that LLMs are not asserters, speakers, or bearers of moral or epistemic responsibility, and he grounds this in 'functional architecture', not in dogmatism. He holds that outputs can function as assertions under four structural conditions and subject to user uptake, which is necessary but not sufficient; some users treat outputs as semantically void, and then the output may fail to function as an assertion (p. 13). He holds that this is a context-bound claim about current systems, not a metaphysical one, and it does not rule out future artificial asserters (p. 17). He explicitly rejects proxy assertion, AI-testimony and proto-assertion as retaining an asserter, though he calls his view 'broadly compatible' with proxy views because it also locates responsibility in humans and institutions (p. 20). He does not claim that function-level assertions are reliable or justified (pp. 14, 17), and he does not offer a theory of responsibility allocation (p. 20). Someone arguing the thesis should not say that he endorses assessing the policy as an asserter, nor that he addresses sycophancy, sampling consistency, or calibration.

> "The core claim is that assertoric function can persist independently of assertoric authority, giving rise to a structurally asymmetric case of assertion without asserter." (Abstract, p. 1) — Shows the paper's central thesis, which denies an asserter and so conflicts with the thesis's policy-level locus.

> "LLMs do not understand what they are, what their outputs mean, or what they are doing. They do not intend, believe, or know in the relevant epistemic sense." (§3, p. 7) — Shows the conservative ontology on which the paper rejects an asserter-level assessment.

> "Since LLMs are not agents, accountability must be grounded in the human and institutional structures that design, deploy, and govern these systems." (§7, p. 19) — Shows that the paper locates accountability in humans and institutions, a rival to assessing at policy level.

> "The normative commitments associated with assertion - responsiveness, answerability, accountability - remain asymmetrically distributed. They do not attach to the machine, but to the human and institutional structures surrounding its deployment." (§6, p. 16) — Shows that the paper denies that assertion's norms (including sincerity) attach to the system.

> "While these accounts highlight important features of human–AI interaction, they typically retain, at some level, the idea that assertion requires an asserter." (§8, p. 21) — Shows that the paper distances itself from views that keep a speaker-like role, which a policy-as-asserter view would be.

> "It also does not, by itself, distinguish between reliable and unreliable assertions." (§5, p. 14) — Shows that the paper explicitly leaves reliability (and so hallucination assessment) to further analysis.

**Caveat.** Full text read (24 pages, published version). The paper does not address sycophancy, sampling or resampling, sincerity assessment of outputs, or calibrated-confidence content, so it bears on the thesis only through its general denial of an asserter and its relocation of accountability to humans.

## Shanahan, Murray, Kyle McDonell & Laria Reynolds (2023). 'Role play with large language models.' Nature 623, 16 November 2023, pp. 493–498. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06647-8

*File: ShanahanMcDonellReynolds2023.pdf — relation to the thesis: CONTRADICTS*

**Argues.** The Perspective proposes role play, and the more nuanced picture of a simulator generating a superposition of simulacra, as the right framing for LLM-based dialogue agents. The aim is to retain folk-psychological vocabulary without anthropomorphism. It argues from how base models are prompted and sampled (the dialogue prompt, autoregressive sampling, the 20-questions example). It then applies the framing to deception (confabulation, 'good faith' falsehood, 'deliberate' falsehood) and to self-preservation and selfhood. It denies that the underlying simulator has beliefs, intentions or goals, and warns that role-played actions can still cause real harm.

**Bearing on the thesis.** (1) Role-play framing of falsehood, pp. 496–497. The authors say that 'it makes little sense to speak of an agent's beliefs or intentions in a literal sense', so the agent 'cannot assert a falsehood in good faith, nor can it deliberately deceive'. Only confabulation applies directly. They then redescribe three cases of false output in role-play terms: confabulation, 'good faith' falsehood (the 2021 World Cup case), and 'deliberate' falsehood (the maliciously prompted car seller). This is a rival to the thesis's 'if outputs are assertions' antecedent, since the authors do not treat outputs as literal assertions. They also evaluate hallucination at the level of the character or role and the simulator, not the trained policy. (2) Resampling, Box 2 and Fig. 3, p. 495. Regenerating the 'revealed' object in 20 questions gives different answers, which the authors take as evidence that the agent never committed to an object ('could not easily be accounted for if the agent genuinely thought of an object'). They treat resampling inconsistency as showing there is no single commitment, not as insincerity. The thesis denies that such inconsistency is evidence of insincerity, so the authors' reading is a rival one: variation across samples is a superposition of characters, not a lie. (3) Level of analysis, p. 496. The simulator has 'no agency of its own', and 'there is no such thing as the true authentic voice of the base model'. Fine-tuning is 'a kind of censorship on the simulator'. The focus is explicitly the base model (Box 1, p. 494), not a fine-tuned policy. (4) Sycophancy and sanction are not discussed. The nearest material is a passing note that RLHF can exacerbate expressed self-preservation (p. 497), and the remark that role-played actions with real effects make the distinction between role-playing and genuine acting 'a little moot', with implications for trustworthiness (p. 496). (5) Calibration, 'p with confidence c': not discussed. Confidence appears only as the 'apparent confidence' of an agent's output.

**What it says on the thesis.** The paper does not anticipate the thesis; it is a rival to answer. It rejects the antecedent that chatbot outputs are literal assertions by an agent with beliefs or intentions (pp. 496–497). It takes resampling inconsistency as evidence against the agent having committed to anything (Box 2), not as neutral on sincerity. It assesses falsehood at the level of role and simulator and does not argue for evaluating a trained policy. It does not discuss sycophancy, sanction, or calibrated 'p with confidence c' content. Its remark that role-played actions have real consequences (p. 496; Conclusion p. 498) is adjacent to the sanction question, but it makes no argument about it. The authors also deny that the simulator has beliefs, so they would reject the claim that the asserted content could be a policy's calibrated credence.

**Actually holds.** The authors do not say LLM dialogue agents lack all folk-psychological properties. They say such language is acceptable when read as role play. Their view is that role-play framing lets us say a dialogue agent 'believes' or 'deceives' in a non-literal sense, with the simulator itself having none of these states. They do not say resampling variation shows dishonesty. Their point is that no single committed answer or character exists in advance. They say fine-tuned agents remain subject to the framing, and that role-played actions can be as harmful as real ones. They explicitly decline to give recommendations (p. 498). They endorse 'shifting freely between multiple metaphors' (p. 493), so one should not present them as insisting on a single framing. They treat the base model as primal, so they do not address a trained, fine-tuned policy as a distinct unit of analysis.

> "it makes little sense to speak of an agent’s beliefs or intentions in a literal sense. So it cannot assert a falsehood in good faith, nor can it deliberately deceive the user." (p. 496, 'Role-playing deception') — Shows the authors deny literal assertion, belief and intention to the agent, which is the thesis's conditional antecedent.

> "This phenomenon could not easily be accounted for if the agent genuinely ‘thought of’ an object at the start of the game." (p. 495, Box 2) — Shows that they read resampling variation as evidence of no prior commitment, not as insincerity.

> "With an LLM-based dialogue agent, it is role play all the way down." (p. 496) — Summarises their anti-literalist stance and rejection of a 'true voice' beneath the role.

> "the distinction between an agent that merely role-plays acting for itself, and one that genuinely acts for itself starts to look a little moot, and this has implications for trustworthiness, reliability and safety." (p. 496) — Shows their only nearby gesture toward consequences and accountability, without any treatment of sanction.

**Caveat.** Full text of the published Nature Perspective was read. The focus is base models, not fine-tuned policies, so the paper's silence on policy-level evaluation, sycophancy, sanction and calibration partly reflects its stated scope.

## Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Santosh S. Vempala and Edwin Zhang, "Why Language Models Hallucinate," arXiv:2509.04664v1 [cs.CL], 4 September 2025 (OpenAI / Georgia Tech).

*File: KalaiEtal2025.pdf — relation to the thesis: SUPPORTS*

**Argues.** Hallucinations are a statistical phenomenon of the trained model's output distribution. In pretraining they arise as errors analogous to binary misclassification, via an 'Is-It-Valid' reduction that lower-bounds the generative error rate by roughly twice the misclassification rate. Birthday-type arbitrary facts give a floor at the 'singleton rate'. They persist after post-training because most benchmarks use binary 0-1 grading, which makes guessing strictly better than abstaining (Observation 1). The authors propose adding explicit confidence thresholds (penalty t/(1−t)) to mainstream evaluations and 'behavioral calibration'. The work is theoretical learning theory plus a short survey of ten benchmarks. It does not discuss assertion, sincerity or speech-act norms.

**Bearing on the thesis.** (1) Unit of assessment. Error, hallucination and calibration are defined over the model's distribution p̂: err = p̂(E) (§3.1, Eq. 1; §3.2 with prompt distribution µ). Hallucination is analysed as a rate and a property of the policy/distribution, not of single utterances. The bounds are on distribution-level rates, and calibration δ is a distribution-level quantity (§3.1). This is compatible with the thesis's policy-level assessment, but the paper never argues that this is the right level for assessing assertions. (2) Calibration. Base models are said to be calibrated after pretraining, while post-trained RL models deviate from calibration (§3.1, Fig. 2). The paper's 'calibration' is the weak, threshold-based δ (and ECE for Fig. 2), not a claim that each output expresses 'p with confidence c'. This bears on the thesis's point that whether the asserted content is the policy's calibrated 'p, with confidence c' is not established. (3) Confidence as expressed in outputs. §4.2 and §5 ('Beyond IDK') distinguish behavioral calibration (the model produces the most useful response it is at least t confident of, so confidence is implicit in what is said) from stating probabilistic confidence. They note that explicit probabilities can be 'unnatural' and mention pragmatics (Austin, Grice) only in passing (§5, p. 16). (4) Incentive/sanction. Binary grading rewards confident guessing and penalizes IDK, so the training and evaluation pressure itself produces bluffing (§1.2, §4.1, App. F). This is a policy-level, incentive-based explanation, relevant to 'sanction'. It is framed in terms of benchmarks, not of any norm of assertion. (5) Resampling inconsistency. Related work (§2, p. 5) notes that inconsistency across answers to related queries is used to detect or mitigate hallucination (Manakul et al.; Xue et al.; Agrawal et al.). The paper's own example of repeated sampling (three different wrong birthdays, ten trials for letter-counting) is used to show error, not to infer insincerity (pp. 1–2). It makes no claim about sincerity either way. (6) Sycophancy. Not discussed; Wei et al. (2023) on sycophancy is cited only as a cause of hallucination ('misleading alignment training', p. 4). (7) Anthropomorphic framing. The test-taker/bluffing analogy (§1.2, §4.1) treats the model as an agent rationally maximizing expected score, but the authors do not draw conclusions about assertion or honesty.

**What it says on the thesis.** The paper does not state, discuss or argue the thesis. It has no treatment of assertion, sincerity, speech-act norms, sycophancy as a separate phenomenon, or sanction. It supplies technical background for two sub-claims. First, hallucination and calibration are naturally analysed as properties of the trained model's distribution, which fits assessment at the policy level. Second, calibration of the model's output distribution is only weakly established, and RL post-training can undermine it, so 'p with confidence c' cannot be read off outputs. Neither point is framed as a claim about what outputs assert. Sycophancy and sanction are not developed. The only gesture toward speech-act theory is the citation of Austin and Grice at p. 16. Inconsistency is mentioned only as a detection signal, not as evidence about sincerity.

**Actually holds.** The authors commit to the following. (a) Hallucination is a plausible falsehood, a special case of generative error, analysable statistically. (b) Errors are expected after pretraining even from error-free data. They are not inevitable for all models: a question-answer database plus IDK can avoid them, but such models are not calibrated (§3.1, 'Hallucinations are inevitable only for base models'). (c) Calibration is a natural consequence of cross-entropy training. Base models are often calibrated, and post-trained models may not be (§3.1, Fig. 2). (d) Persistence after post-training is mainly due to misaligned binary evaluations, so the fix is socio-technical: change existing benchmarks rather than only add hallucination evals. (e) Explicit confidence targets and behavioral calibration are proposed as practical, objective modifications. A careful reader should not attribute to them any view that outputs are assertions, that the model sincerely or insincerely asserts, or that resampling variation is or is not insincerity. They explicitly set aside nuanced pragmatic phenomena (§5, 'Beyond IDK'). Their 'calibration' is a weak threshold-based δ, not full Dawid-style calibration. Their 'bluffing' is an analogy to students, not a claim about speech acts.

> "Indeed, empirical studies (Fig. 2) show that base models are often found to be calibrated, in contrast to post-trained models which may deviate from cross-entropy in favor of reinforcement learning." (§3.1, p. 8) — Shows that the paper treats calibration as a policy-level property that pretraining yields and post-training can undo. This is relevant to the claim that calibrated 'p with confidence c' content is not established.

> "rather than requiring the model to output a probabilistic confidence (Lin et al., 2022a), it must formulate the most useful response in which it is at least t confident." (§4.2, p. 15) — Shows the authors' notion of 'behavioral calibration', in which confidence is realized in what is chosen to be said rather than in an explicitly stated probability.

> "The present paper focuses on the statistical factors regarding the top-level decision of what is said." (§5 'Beyond IDK', p. 16) — Shows that pragmatics and speech-act questions are explicitly bracketed, so the paper cannot be cited as addressing the assertion question.

> "inconsistencies in a model’s answers to semantically related queries can also be leveraged to detect or mitigate hallucinations" (§2 Related work, p. 5) — Shows that resampling or answer inconsistency is treated as a detection signal for hallucination, not as evidence of insincerity.

> "Bluffs are often overconfident and specific, such as “September 30” rather than “Sometime in autumn” for a question about a date." (§1.2, p. 4) — Shows the analogy of model guessing to human bluffing, which is an incentive-based, policy-level account of overconfident output, stopping short of any claim about assertion.

**Caveat.** This is the arXiv v1 preprint (4 Sep 2025). I read the whole text, including the appendices. The paper is a technical learning-theory and evaluation paper that does not engage the philosophy of assertion, so the SUPPORTS verdict concerns only the technical background (policy-level analysis, weak calibration) and not the thesis's central philosophical claim.

## Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn (2025). AI Assertion. Ergo: An Open Access Journal of Philosophy, vol. 12, no. 37, pp. 968–988. https://doi.org/10.3998/ergo.7960

*File: ButlinViebahn2025.pdf — relation to the thesis: ADJACENT*

**Argues.** The paper argues that an entity can assert only if (1) its outputs have a descriptive function and (2) it is sanctionable by the agents it interacts with, because assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained LLMs fail (1), since next-token training does not select outputs for conveying information. Fine-tuned systems (LaMDA, Sparrow) may meet (1) but fail (2), because full sanctioning requires that losing credibility be bad for the asserter, and these systems have no interests. The authors add that AI proxy assertion (Green & Michel's RobotCops) offers no easier route, and that the humans or organisations deploying the systems remain responsible and sanctionable.

**Bearing on the thesis.** The paper does not address the thesis's main claims. It never discusses hallucination or sycophancy as such, resampling or output-to-output inconsistency, insincerity, or whether any asserted content is a calibrated 'p, with confidence c'. It is a rival to the thesis's antecedent, because it denies that current chatbot outputs are assertions (§§2–3, conclusion p. 986). The thesis is conditional and does not assert that antecedent, so the paper is not a rival to the thesis itself. Several points do touch the thesis's sanction component. (a) The treatment of sanctioning for Sparrow and LaMDA is tied to training: weights are fixed at deployment, but 'sensitivity to trust during the training phase could suffice for assertion even in deployment', since deployment outputs are explained partly by earlier training-time sensitivity (p. 982). Sparrow's RLHF reward model is described as the channel through which judgments of incorrectness feed back (pp. 981–982). This gives a passing, implicit pointer toward assessing sanction-sensitivity at the level of the trained system rather than the single output, but it is not argued as a claim about where to assess sanction or hallucination. (b) The sanction analysis has three elements: interlocutors track credibility, the asserter is sensitive to this, and losing credibility is bad for the asserter. The authors conclude that fine-tuned LLMs fail element (iii) (pp. 979–983). So on their view sanction is not even available to the model, which contrasts with a thesis that treats sanction as assessable at policy level conditional on assertion. (c) The proxy section (§4, pp. 984–985) locates sanctionability in the principal (the deploying humans or organisations) and says the proxy may or may not be sanctionable. Organisations 'may often remain sanctionable for the content they (indirectly) put forward'. This is a different locus of assessment from the trained policy. (d) §2.1 (p. 973) says pre-trained outputs are produced 'only because these are among the most likely continuations' and that true outputs reflect true training text. It also notes that fine-tuning for groundedness changes the function of outputs (p. 981), and that some apparent assertions are unverifiable (e.g. 'John baked three cakes last week'). These are about descriptive function, not hallucination or calibration. (e) Footnote 5 (p. 974) distinguishes whether LLM outputs have descriptive functions from whether internal states are descriptive representations. This is the nearest the paper comes to a question about what the content is, and it is unrelated to confidence-qualified content.

**What it says on the thesis.** Not a PRECEDENT or anticipation. The thesis's three components (policy-level assessment of hallucination, sycophancy and sanction; resampling inconsistency not being evidence of insincerity; the open question of calibrated 'p, with confidence c' content) are not raised in the text. The closest overlap is the passage on pp. 981–982 about training-phase sensitivity to trust explaining deployment behaviour.
